description: Biz bilime, teknolojiye ve uzay araştırmalarına meraklı, birlikte üretmeyi seven bir ekibiz. NASA Space Apps için Mars'ta hayatta kalmayı kolaylaştıracak bir rehber ve harita geliştiriyoruz. Ekibimize yazılım, yapay zeka, GIS, tasarım ve astronomiyle ilgilenen, yeni fikirler üretmeyi seven ve öğrenmeye açık kişiler arıyoruz. Amacımız birlikte eğlenerek öğrenmek ve güzel bir proje ortaya çıkarmak! 🚀
summary: SafePath is a layered, interactive 3D map and route planner for astronaut surface excursions in Jezero crater, Mars. Before an astronaut walks to a science target, a small scout rover drives the route first. SafePath combines real NASA data (HiRISE elevation, CTX imagery, THEMIS-derived thermal inertia, Perseverance positions and Navcam photos, MEDA weather and RAD radiation measurements) into one 10 x 10 km mission view. It computes three routes (fastest, most efficient, safest), checks the rover's battery and the astronaut's oxygen for the full round trip, and shows a real Perseverance photo of the destination before departure. When the rover meets an obstacle that orbital data could not show, the D* Lite algorithm repairs the route in real time, so the astronaut walks out and, most importantly, back on a path that has already been tested. Orbital maps cannot see every rock; SafePath moves that risk from the human to the machine.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SafePath is a browser-based mission tool with five screens: a path selector on a rotating Mars globe that flies into Jezero crater, a 3D terrain view with switchable data layers, an astronaut status screen, a simplified tablet view for the astronaut, and a sources page. The user picks a science target, and SafePath computes three routes on a 10 x 10 km grid of real terrain: fastest, most efficient and safest. Each route shows its slope profile, distance, steepest slope and the oxygen and battery left after the round trip.

HOW IT WORKS

1. The scout rover is sent along the selected route first. The astronaut follows its progress on the tablet.

2. At the target, the astronaut sees a real Perseverance Navcam photo taken at that location, so they know what to expect before leaving.

3. On the way back the rover meets an obstacle that is not in the orbital data. It only senses what is within sensor range, and D* Lite repairs the route each time new blocked cells appear.

4. The astronaut then walks the tested and updated route, out and back.

DATA LAYERS

Topographic (HiRISE elevation, resampled to 5 m, and slope), optical (CTX orthoimage), thermal (THEMIS-derived thermal inertia), atmospheric (MEDA air temperature and pressure), radiation (Curiosity RAD measurements) and surface photographs (Perseverance Navcam).

VALIDATION

We compared our elevation grid with the positions recorded by Perseverance inside the mission area: mean difference -0.01 m, standard deviation 0.18 m. Our D* Lite implementation is tested against Dijkstra on random grids, including replanning after hidden obstacles appear.

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS SIMULATED

Real: terrain, slope, imagery, thermal inertia, science stop coordinates, arrival photos, weather and radiation measurements (radiation is from Gale crater, not Jezero), and the route algorithm running on this data. Simulated: rover motion and sensing, the hidden obstacle (placed by us), suit telemetry, and rover mass, speed and battery values, which are placeholders until the rover design is final. Time and energy figures should not be read as results; distances and slopes come directly from the data.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

NASA's first priority is crew safety. SafePath applies the Apollo walk-back rule (never go farther than you can return on foot) to Mars, and adds a rover that takes the unknown risks first. The same approach can serve any site where orbital data is coarser than the hazards.

CREATIVITY

Most maps only show layers. SafePath accepts that the map is incomplete and builds the mission around that fact: the return route matters as much as the way out. The rover is the team's own CAD design.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Matplotlib, pytest, trimesh, cascadio) for the data pipeline and route engine; JavaScript, HTML, CSS and three.js for the interface; Autodesk Fusion for the rover design; GitHub Pages for hosting.
